paragraphs: Friend, here's what this psalm is teaching me. The writer starts by telling his own soul, "Bless the LORD, O my soul!" and he ends the exact same way (Psalm 104:1, 35). In between, he takes a long look at everything God made and sees that none of it runs on its own. The water, the lions, the stork, the sea, all of it depends on Him.

Look at the middle of the psalm. "All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season," and "when You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good things" (Psalm 104:27-28). Every creature gets its place and its food from God's hand, so every creature has a reason to look to Him. And the same hand that feeds them also gives and takes breath: "When You send Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth" (Psalm 104:30). That means your next breath is a gift too, baker, so don't let it go by without a thank-you.

So the writer does what the whole psalm points him toward. "I will sing to the LORD all my life; I will sing praise to my God while I have my being" (Psalm 104:33). He doesn't wait for a perfect day to praise God. He lets what he sees lead him to worship, so when you notice a sunset, a meal or a full breath this week, let it lead you there too. Then say it, just like he did: Bless the LORD, O my soul!
